description: Welcome to our team page! We are a passionate team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are focused on combining software development, design, and interactive storytelling to build innovative solutions using coding, data visualization, and UI/UX design. Excited to collaborate and build something great!
summary:
Rovers, landers and science stations have sat on the Moon and Mars for decades. Each is a real record of a mission, and for a child an open mystery. Today that mystery stays closed: museum labels give one photo and one caption, teachers rebuild every story from scratch, and children aged 6–13 never get to ask what the equipment did or what it found.
RAMIM — Discover the Story. Explore the Science. — is a web experience that turns one space artifact into one interactive story a child can explore.
A child scans a QR code, picks an age band, and reads a short comic built around equipment left on the Moon or Mars. Tapping a glowing hotspot opens a verified NASA fact, a real NASA mission photo or video, or a rotatable 3D model. An AI guide then answers the child's questions in plain language from the same NASA sources, and marks fictional story details as fiction.
Children gain curiosity grounded in real science. Teachers gain a ready-made lesson where every fact carries a NASA source. Museums and outreach teams carry many artifacts on one screen, in more than one language.
In 48 hours we built a working prototype: comic reader, NASA-based hotspots, embedded NASA videos, a 3D model viewer and an AI question guide.
details:
What RAMIM does

RAMIM turns a single piece of space equipment into a single interactive story that a child can explore. A child scans a QR code printed on a museum card, a classroom worksheet or a poster, chooses an age band (8-12, 12–15 or 15–18), and lands in a short digital comic built around one artifact: a science station left on the Moon, a rover on Mars, an instrument that is still sitting there today. The story is the entry point; the science is the payload.

How it works

The comic reader renders the story and overlays hotspots on the equipment in each panel. Every hotspot is bound to a content record that holds a verified NASA fact, a NASA mission photo or video, or a 3D model. Tapping a hotspot opens a card with the fact, the NASA source it comes from, and the media itself; the 3D viewer lets the child rotate the model and see how the parts fit together. At any point the child can ask the AI question guide a question in plain language. The guide receives the question together with the NASA context of the active artifact, answers at the reading level the child selected, stays inside that NASA content, and says explicitly when a detail belongs to the fictional story rather than to science. Characters and story events are fictional and labelled as fiction; equipment, missions, discoveries and media are real and linked to their source.

Benefits and intended impact

Children aged 6–13 currently meet space equipment as one photograph and one caption. RAMIM replaces that with a story they control: they read, tap, explore and ask, so curiosity turns into a question they can actually answer. Teachers get a ready-made lesson in which every fact already carries a NASA source, instead of rebuilding the story themselves. Museums and outreach programmes can put many artifacts on one screen, in more than one language, and add new content without new hardware. The intended impact is a shift in how children encounter space heritage: from looking at an object to understanding what it did, what it found, and why it still matters, and a model in which every artifact already on the Moon and Mars becomes a doorway into real NASA science.

Tools and technologies

We built RAMIM as a browser-based web application so that it runs on the devices children, classrooms and museums already have, with no installation and no special hardware. The prototype was built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, a comic reader and hotspot system we wrote ourselves, an embedded 3D model viewer for rotating the equipment, and a generative AI API for the question guide. NASA facts, photos and videos are linked directly from NASA Science and the NASA Image and Video Library. We used AI-assisted coding and design tools to build the prototype inside the hackathon window, and checked every scientific statement against its NASA source before it shipped.

How it is creative

Most space education content is organised around a mission and reads like a timeline. RAMIM is organised around the object: the artifact is the main character, and its parts are the chapters. A hotspot turns a static image into a question, a QR code turns a physical card or poster into an entrance, and the AI guide turns a child's curiosity into an answer at their own reading level. The creative decision we are proudest of is keeping fiction and science visibly separate: the story can be imaginative precisely because the facts beside it are real and sourced. And because a new artifact is new content rather than new code, the idea scales from one story to a whole museum.

Factors we considered

We designed around the constraints of the people we are serving. For children: short sentences, large tap targets, strong contrast, reading levels instead of a single version, and no accounts, logins or personal data collected. For teachers: facts that are traceable, so a lesson can be defended to a parent or a principal. For museums: deployment on a shared screen or a visitor's own phone, multiple languages, and the ability to add artifacts without rebuilding the product. For trust: a visible source on every hotspot, and an AI that is allowed to explain but not to invent. For reach: a lightweight web app that works on low-bandwidth connections, so the experience is not limited to well-funded institutions.

Honest status

What works today in our prototype: the web app and comic reader, hotspots with NASA-based facts, embedded NASA videos, the 3D model viewer, and the AI question guide. Planned next, and not yet built: more artifact stories, teacher tools, testing with children in classrooms and museums, and printed comics connected through QR codes.
